items.prompt: Kim's gift was well made but unused. What does that show?
choices: Quality measures how well a thing was built, not whether it meets a need
Kim should have chosen a more expensive bottle that held even more water for Ben
Ben was ungrateful and ought to have used the gift anyway
items.explanation: A gift that is well made is always going to be used.

items.prompt: In this unit, what does 'solution' mean?
choices: The correct answer to a test question
The thing someone asks you to build
A fix that real users have already approved
items.explanation: A solution here is the thing requested, as opposed to the problem behind it.

items.prompt: In this unit, what does 'problem' mean?
choices: A bug found in the code after launch by the support team
A complaint the team has decided to ignore
The real difficulty the requested thing should relieve
items.explanation: The problem is the underlying difficulty, not a defect in the build.

items.prompt: Mara asked for a CSV export. What was her real problem?
choices: Noticing early that a number was getting worse
Her spreadsheet program opened files too slowly
The dashboard had no way to be printed on paper
items.explanation: The export was her guess; the problem was early warning of a worsening metric.

items.prompt: What is a CSV file?
choices: A security check applied to exported data before it leaves
A table-like file you can open in a spreadsheet
A button that is added to a dashboard page
items.explanation: A CSV is a plain table-like file that spreadsheets can open.

items.prompt: How should you treat a feature request?
choices: As the final specification to follow exactly
As noise to be filtered out before planning
As a clue to the problem underneath it
items.explanation: The request points toward the problem but is not the problem itself.

items.prompt: What does a request phrased as a solution carry with it?
choices: A hidden guess about what the problem is
A guarantee that the problem will be solved
A complete description of the user's situation
items.explanation: Naming a solution quietly asserts a problem nobody has checked.

items.prompt: Where did the chain from ticket to unused button fail?
choices: The code had bugs that QA failed to catch
No step checked that export served the real need
Priya ignored most of what the ticket text asked her for
items.explanation: Every step was reasonable; the missing step was validating the need.

items.prompt: A team ships a flawless, on-spec feature and usage stays near zero. Which diagnosis fits best?
choices: The spec captured a requested solution nobody had checked against the real problem
QA needed more test cases to find the defect hiding in the release
Users need a training session because the feature is too advanced
The team should have built a faster implementation of the same feature
items.explanation: A correct build only shows the words were followed. The failure sits upstream, where the problem was never validated.
items.reference:
Two different questions
🔧 Built right? Quality: bugs, speed, matching the spec
🎯 Right thing? Fit: does it relieve a real problem
🎁 Ben's bottle: yes to the first, no to the second
Why: quality measures how well something was built, never whether it answers a need.
items.learnMore:
A request is a clue, not a spec

A request phrased as a solution carries a hidden guess about the problem. Building it literally inherits that guess without checking it, so a flawless build can still miss.

Common mistake

Assuming that a clear ticket and a passing test run mean the feature is the right one.
items.reflection: Think of something you were given or built that was done well but never used. What problem was it really meant to solve, and who could have asked about it earlier?

items.prompt: Which request is the clearest sign of an inherited guess rather than a stated problem?
choices: 'Assembling the Monday report takes me an hour of copying numbers between two tools'
'I keep missing the moment a metric starts to turn bad'
'Customers wait too long and nobody on the team hears about it'
'Add an export button', with nothing about what the user does afterward
items.explanation: Only the first names a tool and omits any difficulty. The others each describe something painful that happens to the person.

choices: Team 2 delivered less, so its users see a smaller change in the product after launch

Team 2 knows if the build meets a need; Team 1 only knows it matches the words
Team 2 can skip testing because the underlying need is now confirmed by the requester
items.explanation: Matching the words and meeting the need are different facts; only the question separates them.

items.prompt: Ben asks for a bigger bottle. When is buying exactly that bottle still a good call?
choices: When the bigger bottle costs less than the one he already owns and fits his bag
When asking what it is for confirms that size is really what he lacks
When Ben insists, because the requester always knows what is best
When the shop does not stock any smaller or lighter bottles
items.explanation: Treating a request as a clue does not mean rejecting it; if the check confirms the guess, build it.

items.prompt: Which statement names only a problem?
choices: Ben needs a bigger water bottle
Ben runs out of water on long hikes
Ben needs a bottle with a shoulder strap
items.explanation: Only the first describes a difficulty without naming a thing to buy.

items.prompt: What is the one-sentence test?
choices: State the solution in under ten words, for a busy reader
State who will pay for the finished solution
State the problem without mentioning any solution
items.explanation: The test checks that no solution has sneaked into the problem.

items.prompt: Which statement passes the test?
choices: Mara must notice a worsening metric in time to act
Mara needs a CSV export of the whole ticket dashboard each week
Mara needs a weekly report emailed to her
items.explanation: Only the first leaves a chart, an alert or a file all possible.

items.prompt: What does the five whys technique do?
choices: Asks five different people the same question about the request
Keeps asking what something is for until a need appears
Ranks five possible solutions by their cost
items.explanation: Each answer is checked: need, or just another tool?

items.prompt: What is true about the number five in 'five whys'?
choices: You must ask exactly five times, no more or fewer
Fewer than five questions is never allowed
It is a rule of thumb, not a required count
items.explanation: The goal is reaching a need, however many answers that takes.

items.prompt: In jobs to be done, what does 'job' mean?
choices: The progress someone wants in a particular situation
The person's employment title and level at their company
A task assigned to them by their manager
items.explanation: Job means the progress being sought, not an occupation.

items.prompt: What does a passing problem statement let you do?
choices: Skip talking to the people who actually have the problem
Compare several possible solutions fairly
Pick whichever build is cheapest to make
items.explanation: With no solution inside, many options can be weighed against it.

items.prompt: Does 'Users need a dashboard to track trends' pass the test?
choices: Yes, it names a user and a clear goal
Yes, because dashboards are very common
No, it names the solution (a dashboard)
items.explanation: 'A dashboard' is a solution, so the statement has already chosen one.

items.prompt: Which is the best problem statement for the support team's export request?
choices: Support leads need a chart showing backlog size for each week
Support leads cannot tell early enough that the backlog is getting worse
Support leads need a weekly email that lists the backlog numbers by team and week
Support leads need the export to include an extra date column
items.explanation: The first describes the difficulty only; each other option picks a chart, an email or a file format already.
items.reference:
Does the sentence name a solution?
❌ "Ben needs a bigger bottle" (solution inside)
✅ "Ben runs out of water on long hikes" (difficulty only)
✅ "Mara must notice a worsening metric in time to act"
Why: a statement with no solution in it can be checked against several candidate solutions.
items.learnMore:
The one-sentence problem test

Before building, say the problem in one sentence with no mention of any solution. If you cannot, you do not yet know enough to judge whether the proposed solution is a good one.

Common mistake

Writing 'users need an X so they can Y' and calling it a problem statement; the X is the solution sneaking back in.
items.reflection: Pick a project you are working on. Can you say its problem in one sentence without naming the thing you plan to build?

items.prompt: A statement passes the test. What is the strongest reason that helps before building?
choices: It keeps several candidate solutions open to compare
It guarantees that whichever solution is picked will be adopted
It lets the team stop asking the requester anything further
It shortens the estimate because the scope is now fixed
items.explanation: Passing the test keeps options open; it does not guarantee adoption or fix scope.

It names a group of users instead of one specific person

It presumes filtering is the answer and leaves the difficulty behind it unstated
items.explanation: 'A faster way to filter' is a solution shape; why users filter at all is still unknown.

choices: It hides a solution, since 'better' implies the team should do a redesign

It names no solution but is too vague to rank any options
It is too specific, so it leaves no room for any alternative solutions to compare
items.explanation: A statement must be solution-free and specific enough to rank options.

items.prompt: In the unit's demo model, which depth is the most useful?
choices: No whys at all
As many as 7 whys
About 4 whys
items.explanation: The model peaks near 4, then falls as the statement turns vague.

items.prompt: At 0 whys, the statement is basically:
choices: Build the thing that was literally asked for
Feel in control of your work and your whole career
Notice a trend in time to act
items.explanation: Zero whys means only the literal request.

items.prompt: When does the chain of whys stop?
choices: After exactly five answers have been given, no matter what
When an answer names a need rather than another tool
When the requester starts to get annoyed
items.explanation: The stopping rule is about the type of answer, not the count.

items.prompt: Is 'so I can build a report' a need or a tool?
choices: A need, since it explains the whole request
Neither; it is a complaint about the product
Still a tool, because a report is a solution
items.explanation: A report is one way to serve a need, so keep asking.

items.prompt: What goes wrong with far too many whys?
choices: The statement gets vague and hard to act on
The statement gets more specific every time
The user's original request cancels itself out
items.explanation: Over-abstraction removes the power to choose between options.

items.prompt: Mara's root need after the whys is:
choices: A faster spreadsheet program to open files
Early warning that a trend is getting worse
A better-looking dashboard for the whole team to use
items.explanation: The chain ends at noticing a worsening trend in time.

items.prompt: What does 'validate the problem' mean here?
choices: Run an automated test suite against the code on every change
Get the request approved by the legal team
Confirm with the person that you understood the difficulty
items.explanation: It means checking understanding with the person, not a technical test.

items.prompt: At 3 whys the demo model offers 3 candidate solutions. Which set fits?
choices: A trend chart, an alert, or a weekly summary email
Only the CSV export that was first requested
None, because the statement is too vague
items.explanation: Around 3 whys the statement is specific yet leaves room for several fixes.

items.prompt: A chain runs 'a CSV' → 'to make a report' → 'to know whether the backlog is getting worse'. Which answer is the first to name a need?
choices: 'To make a report' for whoever needs to read it
'A CSV', since it is the thing actually requested
'To know whether the backlog is getting worse'
None of them; every answer is still just a tool
items.explanation: A report and a file are both things to build. Knowing whether the backlog worsens is the difficulty.
items.reference:
Usefulness by whys depth (demo model, illustrative)
0️⃣ 0 whys: 40% useful, only the literal ask
3️⃣ 3 whys: 85% useful, three options to compare
4️⃣ 4 whys: 100% useful, the peak of the model
7️⃣ 7 whys: 25% useful, too broad to decide on
Why: digging helps until the statement becomes too vague to separate good options from bad.
items.learnMore:
Dig until a need appears, then stop

Each answer is a tool or a need. Stop at the first answer that names a need specific enough to compare several solutions; five is a rule of thumb, not a quota.

Common mistake

Going so deep that the answer becomes 'feel in control', which defends any feature and picks none.
items.reflection: Think of a request you made that was really a means to something else. How many whys down was the thing you actually wanted?

items.prompt: In the demo model, 6 whys scores 50% usefulness against 100% at 4 whys, with the same number of options. Best reading?
choices: Usefulness fell because there were fewer candidate solutions left to compare once the chain went past four whys
The extra digging added no new options and cost usefulness as the statement got too broad
Usefulness fell because requesters answered less honestly at greater depth
Six whys is better, since it reaches the most basic need of all
items.explanation: Options stayed flat at 4 while usefulness dropped, so the loss is over-abstraction, not fewer choices.

items.prompt: In jobs to be done, a person 'hires' a product to:
choices: Make progress on a specific job in a situation
Fill an open position on their own team
Reduce the total number of tasks they own at work
items.explanation: 'Hiring' is a metaphor for choosing a product to make progress.

items.prompt: Mara's weekly glance takes roughly:
choices: An hour or more of open-ended analysis
A few seconds of routine attention
A full day of cleaning messy data
items.explanation: Her job is a quick, routine look at the trend.

items.prompt: Which solution best fits the weekly glance?
choices: A raw data export that she must open
A custom query editor with many options
A trend line already visible on the dashboard
items.explanation: A glance needs the answer in front of her with zero steps.

items.prompt: Which solution best fits the deep dive?
choices: Raw data to slice and filter freely
A fixed chart drawn in advance
A single color-coded status light on the home page
items.explanation: An open question needs data nobody pre-arranged.

items.prompt: Why does context matter for picking a solution?
choices: Context only changes the color of buttons
The same need can call for different solutions
Needs change every time the data refreshes
items.explanation: Different situations put different demands on the solution.

items.prompt: What does a raw file add to a routine glance?
choices: Security to the dashboard being used
Speed through caching of the numbers
Friction to something that should be instant
items.explanation: Opening a file is extra work for a few-second check.

items.prompt: Why can't a pre-drawn chart serve the deep dive?
choices: An open 'why' needs data nobody anticipated
Charts are always less accurate than tables
Charts cannot show values from each week
items.explanation: A fixed picture cannot answer a question it was not drawn for.

items.prompt: Which need did both jobs in the unit share?
choices: Deleting old tickets in bulk
Seeing a number over time
Switching to a dark color scheme
items.explanation: Both involve the same underlying data over time.

items.prompt: Same need: 'see a number over time'. Which pairing of job and solution is right?
choices: Daily five-second check gets raw rows; a deep audit gets a fixed picture of last month's total
Both jobs get a single export, which keeps the product simple
Daily check gets raw rows; the deep audit gets a color-coded light
Daily five-second check gets a line on the home screen; a deep audit gets raw rows
items.explanation: Each solution should match the attention and openness the job demands.
items.reference:
One need, two jobs
⏱️ Weekly glance: a few seconds, routine → trend line on the dashboard
🔍 Deep dive: rare, an hour of analysis → raw data to slice freely
📄 One generic file fits the second job and fails the first
Why: the situation, not just the data, decides which solution fits.
items.learnMore:
Name the job, then pick the solution

People hire a product to make progress on a job in a situation. The same underlying need can sit inside very different jobs, and a solution tuned for one works against the other.

Common mistake

Choosing a solution from the data alone ('they need these numbers') without asking in what situation they will use them.
items.reflection: Think of a tool you use for two quite different purposes. Where does it fit one job well and the other badly?

items.prompt: A feature built for one job is applied to a different job. What usually happens?
choices: It works equally well, because the underlying data is the same in both
It improves, because broader features cover more situations at once
It adds friction or blocks needed freedom, since the jobs ask for opposite things
It breaks, because the data formats differ between the two jobs
items.explanation: Same data does not mean same demands; a solution optimized for one can work against the other.

items.prompt: What was the root need behind the bulk delete request?
choices: Agents wanted to erase the history of every customer
The queue did not separate actionable tickets from the rest
The database was running out of room to store tickets
items.explanation: The whys traced the ask to queue clutter.

items.prompt: What is a destructive action?
choices: One that makes a page load more slowly
One that only administrators are allowed to see
One that can erase information or cause damage
items.explanation: Destructive means the harm from a mistake can be hard to undo.

items.prompt: What did the team ship instead of bulk delete?
choices: A default status filter with a show-all toggle
A multi-select screen with a delete endpoint
A nightly job that purges old tickets
items.explanation: The filter hides closed tickets by default and can be turned off.

items.prompt: Why does a filter beat bulk delete in this story?
choices: It is faster than every other possible feature
It solves the clutter with no data loss
Agents never need to look at closed tickets
items.explanation: Hiding keeps the records and still clears the queue.

items.prompt: Which protections does a safe bulk delete need?
choices: A brighter color on the delete button itself
A longer maximum length for the ticket title
A confirmation, an undo window and an audit log
items.explanation: Mistakes touch many records, so safeguards matter.

items.prompt: What does a literal build of the ticket produce?
choices: A multi-select screen and a delete-many endpoint
A filter on ticket status for the queue
A new category for sorting tickets
items.explanation: Built as written, it is exactly a bulk delete.

items.prompt: The reframe changes the question from 'how to delete faster' to:
choices: How to store a larger number of tickets cheaply
How to keep the queue showing only actionable tickets
How to hire extra agents to clear the queue
items.explanation: The question became about what the queue displays.

items.prompt: Did the whys argue the agents out of their request?
choices: Yes, the request was cancelled outright
Yes, the agents were told to stop asking
No, they found a fit for the real need
items.explanation: The need was kept; only the solution changed.

items.prompt: After the reframe, which risk from the original ask disappears?
choices: One mistaken click erasing many records with no way back
Agents needing a short tutorial for the new queue filter
Slower page loads from rendering a long list of tickets
Disagreement over which tickets should count as closed
items.explanation: A hide-by-default filter keeps every record, so irreversible loss is gone.
items.reference:
Same ticket, two builds
🎫 Ask: "We need bulk delete"
🛠️ Literal: multi-select + delete endpoint + confirmation, undo, audit log
🎯 Reframed: default status filter + show-all toggle, no data loss
Why: the whys found a clutter problem, and clutter is solved by hiding, not destroying.
items.learnMore:
Reframe the question, not just the feature

Asking why moved the question from destroying records faster to keeping the queue showing only actionable tickets. A destructive build needs extra safeguards; a filter needs none.

Common mistake

Reading the reframe as 'we talked the users out of it' when it actually met their need with less risk.

The ask was a clue; the filter meets the underlying clutter need with less risk
items.explanation: Serving the need is how users are respected, not building the words as written.

If records must truly be erased, such as personal data to remove
If agents simply prefer the word 'delete' to the word 'hide' on the page
items.explanation: Pain from clutter pointed to hiding; a real need to erase would justify the destructive build.

items.prompt: What was User A's need behind dark mode?
choices: A look that matches other tools
A purely aesthetic preference
Less eye strain in low light
items.explanation: A used the product at night and the bright screen hurt.

items.prompt: What was User B's need behind dark mode?
choices: To match expectations set by other tools
To reduce eye strain in low light
To protect the data stored in the product
items.explanation: B felt the product looked dated next to other tools.

items.prompt: What was User C's need behind dark mode?
choices: A fix for a pattern of support complaints
A simple preference for how it looks
A way to save battery on every device
items.explanation: C had no functional pain, only taste.

items.prompt: Which requester matched a support-ticket pattern?
choices: User B, who found the look dated
User C, who just liked the look
User A, with the eye strain at night
items.explanation: A's complaint lined up with repeated 'hard to use at night' tickets.

items.prompt: What is a support-ticket pattern?
choices: Several help requests pointing at the same repeated pain
A template that agents use to answer every ticket
A report showing how many tickets each agent closed
items.explanation: A pattern is repeated pain seen across several requests.

items.prompt: What does prioritization mean?
choices: Building every request in the order it arrived
Deciding what to build first when you can't build everything
Asking users to vote on which feature they like best
items.explanation: Not everything fits, so choosing order matters.

items.prompt: What is a roadmap?
choices: A map of how the product's screens connect
A record of bugs that have already been fixed
The ordered list of work the team plans to do
items.explanation: The roadmap is the planned order of upcoming work.

items.prompt: Why trace the whys per requester?
choices: One feature name can hide different needs
Every requester always has the same reason
It saves the team from building anything at all
items.explanation: The reasons behind identical requests can differ in weight.

items.prompt: Which requester deserves the earliest slot on the roadmap?
choices: A user who finds the old look dated compared with several rival tools they use
A user whose night-time eye strain matches repeated support complaints
A user who prefers dark themes in every app, phone setting and website they use
A user who happened to post the request first in the feedback thread last month
items.explanation: Real usability pain backed by a support pattern carries the highest cost of waiting.
items.reference:
Three requesters, one feature name
🌙 A: eye strain at night, matches a support pattern → highest weight
🪞 B: other tools have it → expectation gap
🎨 C: just prefers the look → lowest urgency
Why: the same words can hide needs of very different weight.
items.learnMore:
Trace the whys per requester

One feature name can cover several different needs. Weighing the real cost of not building for each need is how you sequence work fairly.

Common mistake

Assuming everyone who asked for the same feature has the same reason, so the one with real pain is lost in the count.
items.reflection: Think of a request you've heard from several people. Would each of them give the same reason if you asked?

items.prompt: What did the whys reveal that the feature name 'dark mode' could not?
choices: The requesters carried needs of quite different weight
That dark mode was technically too hard for the team to build
That every requester wanted it for the same reason
That the support tickets were unrelated to the requests
items.explanation: The name looked identical across requesters; the reasons were not.

items.prompt: Twenty people ask for dark mode, and every one gives a taste reason with no pain. How does that change the call?
choices: Twenty requests automatically outrank a single request that cites a real pain point
Taste reasons are invalid, so all twenty requests should be dropped
The roadmap order must follow the vote count exactly as tallied
Weight comes from the need behind the request; volume adds visibility, not urgency
items.explanation: Counting voices is not the same as weighing needs, though volume can still shape effort later.

items.prompt: Why sample real requesters instead of assuming one shared reason?
choices: Sampling is quicker than building the feature for all of them
Requesters usually refuse to answer questions about their request when asked directly
An assumed reason can hide the person with real pain, or invent one nobody holds
Assuming is fine so long as the feature itself is small
items.explanation: Only asking shows which needs exist and which carry weight.

items.prompt: What is the fix for guessing the whys in a meeting?
choices: Ask the person who filed the request
Hold a longer meeting with the whole team
Write the guesses down more clearly
items.explanation: Real answers come from the requester, not from the team's guesses.

items.prompt: What is the problem with stopping at the first why?
choices: The requester will have lost interest by then
The answer is often still a solution
The team has used up its allowed questions
items.explanation: 'So I can build a report' still names a tool.

items.prompt: What should the aim of the whys be?
choices: To prove that the request was unnecessary
To make the requester explain themselves fully
To find the solution that fits the need
items.explanation: The goal is a better fit, not winning an argument.

items.prompt: A tiny, easily reversed tweak should get:
choices: A light check, not a full interrogation
The same full interrogation as a big feature
No thought at all before building it
items.explanation: Effort should match the cost and risk of the build.

items.prompt: A destructive, hard-to-reverse feature should get:
choices: A quick check, since users asked for it
Deeper digging before anything is built
A decision from the loudest requester
items.explanation: High stakes call for more scrutiny of the need.

items.prompt: Which one is a failure mode of the technique?
choices: Asking the requester directly about their need
Naming the need before choosing a solution
Concluding 'nobody needs this' as the goal
items.explanation: Using the whys to dismiss requests misuses them.

items.prompt: Why scale the digging to cost and risk?
choices: Heavy process on cheap changes wastes time
Cheap changes never have any need behind them
Risky changes should be built before asking anything
items.explanation: Spend scrutiny where a mistake would be costly.

items.prompt: Which failure mode is 'so I can build a report'?
choices: Guessing the whys in a meeting
Stopping at the first why
Applying equal rigor to every request
items.explanation: The answer is still a solution, so the chain stopped too soon.

items.prompt: A team spends an hour brainstorming reasons for a request and writes whys on a whiteboard without contacting the requester. Main risk?
choices: They will ask so many whys that the problem turns vague
They will skip prioritization of the work entirely
They solve a plausible problem that may not be the requester's
They will build a destructive feature by default
items.explanation: Invented answers feel convincing but are guesses about someone else's situation.
items.reference:
Four ways the technique goes wrong
🗣️ Guessing the whys in a meeting without asking
🛑 Stopping at the first why (a report is still a tool)
🙅 Using it to talk users out of the request
⚖️ Same rigor for a tiny tweak and a risky build
Why: ask the actual requester, reach a need, find a fit, and scale the effort to the stakes.
items.learnMore:
The technique needs judgment

The whys only help when real requesters answer, when the chain reaches a need, when the aim is a better fit, and when the effort matches the cost and risk of the build.

Common mistake

Applying the same long interrogation to every request, or treating it as a way to say no.
items.reflection: Think of a process you've seen followed rigidly. Where did following it exactly cost more than it protected?

items.prompt: Which request merits the lightest whys treatment?
choices: Auto-deleting accounts that have been inactive for a full year without warning
Changing the color of a button, which can be undone in minutes
Rebuilding how permissions are granted to every user across all teams
Charging users for an export that used to be free of charge for everyone
items.explanation: Cheap, reversible changes need little digging; the others carry real risk.
